COPYRIGHT STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS AND THE DAMAGES LOOKBACK (17 U.S.C. § 507; PETRELLA; WARNER CHAPPELL MUSIC V. NEALY) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · Harbor Street Publishing, LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS COPYRIGHT LIMITATIONS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the time limits that the federal Copyright Act places on infringement actions, and the separate question of how far back in time a plaintiff with a timely claim may recover money. It sets out the text of 17 U.S.C. section 507; the Supreme Court's account in Petrella v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Inc. of when a copyright claim accrues, of the separate-accrual rule, and of the unavailability of laches against a claim for damages filed inside the three-year window; the Supreme Court's 2024 holding in Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy that the Act contains no separate three-year cap on monetary recovery; the question about the discovery rule that both opinions expressly left open; the Ninth Circuit's position in Starz Entertainment, LLC v. MGM Domestic Television Distribution, LLC, which governs federal district courts in California; and, by way of contrast, the express six-year damages limitation Congress wrote into the Patent Act. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning a work of Harbor Street Publishing, LLC described as follows: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. The earliest infringing conduct presently suspected is believed to have begun on or about June 2014, and the owner states that it first learned of facts suggesting infringement on or about February 3, 2026. This Information Sheet reports what the statute and the cited opinions say. It does not determine when any claim accrued, whether any claim is timely, how far back any recovery could reach, or whether any tolling or equitable doctrine applies in a particular dispute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE THREE-YEAR PERIOD FOR CIVIL COPYRIGHT ACTIONS (17 U.S.C. § 507(B))
The Copyright Act sets a single time limit for civil actions. Section 507(b) provides that no civil action may be maintained under the title unless it is commenced within three years after the claim accrued. The sentence is written as a limit on when suit may be brought; by its terms it fixes a period measured from accrual of the claim, and it says nothing on its face about how much of a plaintiff's loss may be recovered once a suit is timely brought. The provision applies to civil actions under Title 17 generally, not only to infringement claims. What the word 'accrued' means in this sentence, and whether the Act permits accrual to be measured from the plaintiff's discovery of the infringement rather than from the infringing act, are addressed in the clauses that follow.

THE FIVE-YEAR PERIOD FOR CRIMINAL PROCEEDINGS, AND THE UNCORRECTED 1976 HOUSE REPORT NOTE (17 U.S.C. § 507(A))
Subsection (a) of the same section governs criminal proceedings. As amended, it provides that, except as expressly provided otherwise in the title, no criminal proceeding may be maintained unless it is commenced within five years after the cause of action arose. The subsection has not always read that way: the amendment notes printed with the section record that in 1997 Congress substituted '5' for 'three' in subsection (a), and that in 1998 Congress added the opening 'Except as expressly provided otherwise in this title' clause. The Historical and Revision Notes reproduced under the section, drawn from House Report No. 94-1476 accompanying the 1976 general revision, still describe section 507 as establishing a three-year period for both criminal proceedings and civil actions. The two criminal and civil periods are therefore now different lengths, and are measured from different events -- five years from when the cause of action arose for criminal proceedings, three years from when the claim accrued for civil actions.

WHEN A COPYRIGHT CLAIM ACCRUES: THE INCIDENT-OF-INJURY RULE (PETRELLA)
Because section 507(b) runs from accrual, the Supreme Court in Petrella v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Inc. began with what accrual means. The Court restated the ordinary rule that a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action, explaining that the limitations period generally begins to run at the point when the plaintiff can file suit and obtain relief. Applying that ordinary rule to copyright, the Court wrote that a copyright claim thus arises or accrues when an infringing act occurs. That formulation is commonly called the incident-of-injury rule. The Court's later opinion in Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy repeated the same sentence from Petrella when describing 'one understanding' of section 507(b).

THE SEPARATE-ACCRUAL RULE: EACH INFRINGING ACT STARTS ITS OWN CLOCK (PETRELLA)
Petrella described a rule that the Court said is widely recognized as attending the copyright statute of limitations: the separate-accrual rule. Under it, when a defendant commits successive violations, the limitations period runs separately from each violation. Each reproduction or distribution of an infringing work is a new wrong that gives rise to a discrete claim, so each infringing act starts a new limitations period. The Court drew the practical consequence in the same passage: under the three-year provision an infringement is actionable within three years, and only three years, of its occurrence. A course of continuing infringement is therefore not treated as one indivisible wrong that accrues once; it is treated as a series of separately accruing claims.

THE DISCOVERY RULE IS WIDELY APPLIED BUT THE SUPREME COURT HAS NOT DECIDED WHETHER THE ACT ALLOWS IT
Alongside the incident-of-injury rule, most federal Courts of Appeals apply a discovery rule, under which the limitations period starts when the plaintiff discovers, or with due diligence should have discovered, the injury that forms the basis for the claim. Petrella recorded that practice in a footnote and stated in the same breath that the Supreme Court had not passed on the question, counting nine Courts of Appeals as having adopted the rule. Ten years later, in Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy, the Court repeated that it has never decided whether that assumption is valid -- whether a copyright claim accrues when a plaintiff discovers or should have discovered an infringement, rather than when the infringement happened -- and described the count of Courts of Appeals applying a copyright discovery rule as eleven at last count. The Nealy Court explained that the issue was not properly presented because the defendant had never challenged the discovery rule's use below. The availability of the discovery rule under the Copyright Act therefore remains an open question at the Supreme Court.

LACHES CANNOT BAR A DAMAGES CLAIM BROUGHT INSIDE THE THREE-YEAR WINDOW (PETRELLA)
The question presented in Petrella was whether laches -- unreasonable, prejudicial delay in commencing suit -- may bar relief on a copyright infringement claim brought within the three-year limitations period. The Court held that laches cannot be invoked to preclude adjudication of a claim for damages brought within the three-year window, reasoning that when Congress has fixed the timeliness of suit, courts are not at liberty to jettison that judgment. The Court drew a line for equitable relief: in extraordinary circumstances, laches may bar at the very threshold the particular relief the plaintiff requests, and a plaintiff's delay can in any event be taken into account at the remedial stage in shaping injunctive relief and in assessing the infringer's profits. The holding concerns the equitable defense of laches; it does not address equitable estoppel, which the Court treated separately.

NO SEPARATE THREE-YEAR CAP ON MONETARY RECOVERY (WARNER CHAPPELL MUSIC, INC. V. NEALY)
In Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy the Supreme Court took up a question left over from the spread of the discovery rule: if a plaintiff's claim for an old infringement is timely because he discovered it recently, may he nonetheless be barred from recovering money for infringements that occurred more than three years before suit? The Court assumed without deciding that a claim is timely under section 507(b) if brought within three years of discovery, then held that no such limit on damages exists. Reading the statute, the Court described section 507(b) as establishing a three-year period for filing suit that begins to run when a claim accrues and observed that the clock it sets is a singular one. The Court summarized its conclusion by saying that the Copyright Act entitles a copyright owner to recover damages for any timely claim.

WHERE A DAMAGES LIMIT WOULD HAVE TO COME FROM: THE REMEDIAL SECTIONS (17 U.S.C. § 504; NEALY)
The Nealy Court reasoned that if any time limit on damages exists it must come from the Act's remedial sections rather than from the limitations provision. Section 504(a) provides that, with exceptions stated elsewhere in the title, an infringer of copyright is liable for either the copyright owner's actual damages and any additional profits of the infringer, as provided by subsection (b), or statutory damages, as provided by subsection (c). The Court read those provisions as stating without qualification that an infringer is liable for one or the other, and concluded that there is no time limit on monetary recovery, so that a copyright owner possessing a timely claim for infringement is entitled to damages no matter when the infringement occurred. The Court added that it rejected applying a judicially invented damages limit to convert one accrual rule into the other.

THE 'THREE YEARS BACK' SENTENCE IN PETRELLA AND HOW NEALY READ IT
Petrella contains a sentence that was read for a decade as describing a damages lookback: summarizing Congress's two time prescriptions, the Court wrote that section 507(b)'s limitations period allows plaintiffs during the lengthy copyright term to gain retrospective relief running only three years back from the date the complaint was filed. In Nealy the Court explained what that sentence had meant. It said that in making the statement it had merely described how the limitations provision works when a plaintiff has no timely claims for infringing acts more than three years old -- the situation in Petrella, where the plaintiff had long known of the infringing conduct and sued only for infringements within the preceding three years -- and that it had not gone beyond the facts of that case to say that a plaintiff with a timely claim for an earlier infringement may not obtain monetary relief.

Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Thomas and Justice Alito, dissented in Nealy on the ground that the Court had sidestepped the logically antecedent question whether the Copyright Act has room for a discovery rule, writing that the Act almost certainly does not tolerate one. The Court drew a line for equitable relief: in extraordinary circumstances, laches may bar at the very threshold the particular relief the plaintiff requests, and a plaintiff's delay can in any event be taken into account at the remedial stage in shaping injunctive relief and in assessing the infringer's profits. The holding concerns the equitable defense of laches; it does not address equitable estoppel, which the Court treated separately.

expectedJSON.body: In Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy the Supreme Court took up a question left over from the spread of the discovery rule: if a plaintiff's claim for an old infringement is timely because he discovered it recently, may he nonetheless be barred from recovering money for infringements that occurred more than three years before suit? The Court assumed without deciding that a claim is timely under section 507(b) if brought within three years of discovery, then held that no such limit on damages exists. Reading the statute, the Court described section 507(b) as establishing a three-year period for filing suit that begins to run when a claim accrues and observed that the clock it sets is a singular one. The Court summarized its conclusion by saying that the Copyright Act entitles a copyright owner to recover damages for any timely claim.

expectedJSON.body: The Nealy Court reasoned that if any time limit on damages exists it must come from the Act's remedial sections rather than from the limitations provision. Section 504(a) provides that, with exceptions stated elsewhere in the title, an infringer of copyright is liable for either the copyright owner's actual damages and any additional profits of the infringer, as provided by subsection (b), or statutory damages, as provided by subsection (c). The Court read those provisions as stating without qualification that an infringer is liable for one or the other, and concluded that there is no time limit on monetary recovery, so that a copyright owner possessing a timely claim for infringement is entitled to damages no matter when the infringement occurred. The Court added that it rejected applying a judicially invented damages limit to convert one accrual rule into the other.

expectedJSON.body: Petrella contains a sentence that was read for a decade as describing a damages lookback: summarizing Congress's two time prescriptions, the Court wrote that section 507(b)'s limitations period allows plaintiffs during the lengthy copyright term to gain retrospective relief running only three years back from the date the complaint was filed. expectedJSON.body: The rule the Supreme Court rejected in Nealy came from the Second Circuit. As the Nealy opinion recounts the procedural history, the district court, relying on a decision from the Second Circuit, held that even when claims for old infringements are timely, monetary relief is limited to the three years prior to the filing of the action; the Nealy opinion identifies that decision as Sohm v. The Eleventh Circuit decision the Supreme Court affirmed, 60 F.4th 1325, had aligned itself with the Ninth rather than the Second Circuit.

expectedJSON.body: Federal district courts in California sit within the Ninth Circuit, which addressed both halves of this problem in Starz Entertainment, LLC v. MGM Domestic Television Distribution, LLC. The panel held that the discovery rule for accrual allows copyright holders to recover damages for all infringing acts that occurred before they knew or reasonably should have known of the infringing incidents, and that the three-year limitations period runs from the date the claim accrued -- that is, from the date when the copyright holder knew or should have known of the infringement. The panel closed by stating its agreement with the district court that the discovery rule of accrual of copyright claims is alive and well. The Supreme Court's later opinion in Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy cited Starz when describing the Eleventh Circuit's decision to ally itself with the Ninth rather than the Second Circuit, and affirmed that Eleventh Circuit judgment.

expectedJSON.body: Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Thomas and Justice Alito, dissented in Nealy on the ground that the Court had sidestepped the logically antecedent question whether the Copyright Act has room for a discovery rule, writing that the Act almost certainly does not tolerate one. The dissent reasoned from the general presumption that a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action, and from the Court's prior statements that unless the statute at hand directs otherwise, courts proceed consistent with traditional equitable practice and ordinarily apply the discovery rule only in cases of fraud or concealment. The dissenters would have dismissed the writ as improvidently granted and awaited a case squarely presenting the question whether the Copyright Act authorizes the discovery rule. A dissent binds no court; it is reported here because it identifies the question the majority reserved.

expectedJSON.body: The Patent Act shows what an express statutory limit on recovery looks like. Section 286 provides that, except as otherwise provided by law, no recovery may be had for any infringement committed more than six years prior to the filing of the complaint or counterclaim for infringement in the action. That sentence limits recovery by reference to the date of the infringing conduct; section 507(b) of the Copyright Act, by contrast, limits the time for commencing an action by reference to accrual of the claim. In SCA Hygiene Products Aktiebolag v. First Quality Baby Products, LLC, the Supreme Court applied the reasoning of Petrella to section 286, recalling that in Petrella it had held that laches cannot preclude a claim for damages incurred within the Copyright Act's three-year limitations period, and holding that laches likewise cannot be interposed as a defense against damages where the infringement occurred within the period prescribed by section 286.
